title: Agile Principles
summary: Values and principles for developing software through collaboration, working outcomes, customer partnership, and adaptation instead of rigid prediction.
description: Agile is not a prescribed process, job title, or meeting schedule. It is a value system for making better software decisions under uncertainty. Teams still need an explicit method, technical discipline, product judgment, and organizational support to turn those values into useful delivery.
bestFor: Product or software work where learning changes the plan
Cross-functional teams able to collaborate frequently
Environments where useful increments and feedback can be delivered
avoidWhen: Work whose scope and sequence are legally or physically fixed
Organizations using the label only to demand more output without autonomy
coreIdeas: Prefer people and interactions while still using useful processes and tools
Deliver working software as the primary progress signal
Collaborate with customers throughout the work
Respond to evidence and change instead of protecting an obsolete plan

flow.title: Frame the outcome
flow.description: Agree on the user or business outcome, current evidence, constraints, and the smallest useful learning target.

flow.title: Build a useful increment
flow.description: Collaborate across disciplines to produce a small working slice rather than completing disconnected functional phases.

flow.title: Seek feedback
flow.description: Review the working result with users, stakeholders, telemetry, and operational evidence instead of relying on plan completion.

flow.title: Adapt direction and practice
flow.description: Update priorities, design, implementation, or team practices according to what was learned and the remaining risks.

roles: No mandatory roles are prescribed by Agile itself
Product, design, engineering, quality, and stakeholder roles collaborate according to the context
strengths: Makes learning and customer value central
Supports adaptation before large investments are locked in
Encourages cross-functional ownership
risks: Can become a vague label with no operating rules
May be misused to avoid planning, documentation, or accountability
Local team agility cannot overcome every organizational dependency
healthySignals: Useful software reaches users regularly
Plans change when evidence changes
Teams improve both product and process

title: Scrum Framework
summary: A lightweight framework for complex product work using a Product Goal, ordered Product Backlog, timeboxed Sprints, defined accountabilities, and empirical inspection.
description: Scrum provides a minimal container rather than a complete delivery system. Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers collaborate around a Product Goal; each Sprint creates a valuable usable Increment and opportunities to inspect and adapt. Engineering practices, discovery, organizational design, and release strategy still need deliberate choices.
bestFor: Complex product work benefiting from a stable cross-functional team
Teams able to pursue a coherent Product Goal
Organizations willing to inspect evidence and change plans
avoidWhen: Work is passed between functional silos with no shared ownership
Events are required but teams lack authority to improve the system
coreIdeas: Empiricism through transparency, inspection, and adaptation
A small self-managing Scrum Team owns the work
Each Sprint pursues a Sprint Goal and produces a usable Increment
Artifacts carry commitments: Product Goal, Sprint Goal, and Definition of Done

flow.title: Set Product Goal
flow.description: The Product Owner and team maintain a long-term objective that gives the Product Backlog direction and coherence.

flow.title: Sprint Planning
flow.description: The Scrum Team selects a valuable Sprint objective, forecasts work, and creates a plan for delivering a usable Increment.

flow.title: Daily progress and adaptation
flow.description: Developers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal every day and adapt the plan while doing design, development, testing, and integration.

flow.title: Sprint Review
flow.description: The Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the outcome, discuss environmental changes, and adapt the Product Backlog.

flow.title: Sprint Retrospective
flow.description: The Scrum Team inspects how it worked and plans a concrete improvement to increase quality and effectiveness.

cadence: Sprints of one month or less
Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective every Sprint
strengths: Creates a regular inspect-and-adapt rhythm
Clarifies product, facilitation, and delivery accountabilities
Keeps a stable goal while allowing the plan to change
risks: Can degrade into ceremony compliance
Separate component teams can produce incomplete increments
Sprint commitments may be mistaken for fixed scope guarantees
healthySignals: Each Sprint produces a usable Increment
Sprint Goals guide decisions during change
Retrospectives create completed improvements

title: Kanban Method
summary: A flow-based method that makes work visible, controls work in progress, actively manages items, and improves a service through evidence and experiments.
description: Kanban begins with the current workflow rather than requiring a new set of roles or iterations. Teams define workflow states and policies, limit work in progress, measure flow, and evolve the service. It can support product development, operations, support, recruitment, or any knowledge-work system.
bestFor: Teams with continuously arriving work
Services where flow time and predictability matter
Existing processes that need evolutionary improvement
avoidWhen: Leaders refuse to respect work-in-progress limits
The board is treated as a task display without flow policies or metrics
coreIdeas: Define and visualize the workflow explicitly
Control work in progress to protect flow
Manage work items actively rather than only managing people
Use flow measures and feedback to improve predictability

flow.title: Define the workflow
flow.description: Map how a work item moves from commitment to delivery, including states, policies, classes of service, and completion rules.

flow.title: Pull within limits
flow.description: Start new work only when capacity exists under explicit work-in-progress controls instead of maximizing individual utilization.

flow.title: Manage active items
flow.description: Review aging, blockage, dependencies, and service expectations so items finish rather than merely move between people.

flow.title: Review flow and improve
flow.description: Use throughput, work-item age, cycle time, and service-level expectations to run safe process experiments.

roles: No prescribed roles are required to begin using Kanban
Existing service delivery and organizational roles operate and improve the workflow
cadence: Periodic service delivery and operations review
strengths: Fits continuous and unpredictable demand
Makes bottlenecks and aging visible
Allows gradual change without reorganizing roles first
risks: A board alone creates no flow discipline
Too many exceptions can defeat work-in-progress controls
Optimizing one board may shift delay elsewhere
healthySignals: Work finishes faster and more predictably
Blocked and aging items trigger action
Policies and limits are understood and respected

references.name: Lean Enterprise Institute: What is Lean Thinking?

title: Waterfall Delivery Model
summary: A sequential delivery model that progresses through substantially completed analysis, design, implementation, verification, and release phases.
description: Waterfall seeks predictability by defining requirements and plans early, then moving work through controlled phases. It can be appropriate where change is unusually expensive, evidence must be approved at formal gates, or physical and regulatory dependencies dominate. It becomes risky when early assumptions cannot be validated until late.
bestFor: Stable requirements with costly downstream change
Regulated or contractual environments requiring formal phase evidence
Projects dominated by physical procurement or sequential dependencies
avoidWhen: User needs and technical feasibility are highly uncertain
Value can be tested through small working increments much earlier
coreIdeas: Define scope and acceptance before major implementation
Complete and approve phase outputs at explicit gates
Manage change through formal impact assessment
Use traceability from requirements through verification

flow.title: Requirements
flow.description: Document intended scope, constraints, acceptance conditions, dependencies, and governance before detailed solution work.

flow.title: Solution design
flow.description: Produce architecture, interaction, data, integration, and operational designs that satisfy the approved requirement baseline.

flow.title: Implementation
flow.description: Build the approved solution according to the design and controlled change process.

flow.title: Verification
flow.description: Test the complete system against traced requirements and resolve deviations before release approval.

flow.title: Release and maintenance
flow.description: Deploy or hand over the approved solution, operate it, and manage subsequent changes through maintenance processes.

strengths: Supports formal traceability and approvals
Can coordinate expensive sequential dependencies
Creates explicit scope and governance baselines
risks: Important feedback arrives late
Phase handoffs can fragment ownership
Formal change control may protect a flawed original assumption
healthySignals: Requirements are genuinely stable and testable
Phase evidence is reviewed rather than rubber-stamped
Risks and changes are surfaced transparently

title: Scrumban Hybrid
summary: A pragmatic hybrid that retains useful Scrum cadences or goals while applying Kanban flow visualization, work-in-progress limits, and pull policies.
description: Scrumban is not a single official framework. Teams commonly use it when Sprint-based planning is helpful but demand, support work, or bottlenecks require stronger flow management. The operating rules must be written explicitly so the hybrid does not become an arbitrary mixture of ceremonies.
bestFor: Scrum teams struggling with carryover and excessive concurrent work
Teams mixing planned product work with urgent service demand
Organizations transitioning gradually from iterations toward flow
avoidWhen: The team cannot explain which Scrum or Kanban rules it follows
The hybrid is used to avoid clear goals, policies, or accountability
coreIdeas: Keep only cadences that provide useful feedback
Visualize the actual workflow rather than a generic to-do list
Use explicit pull and work-in-progress policies
Review both goal progress and flow evidence

flow.title: Set goal and flow policies
flow.description: Agree which Sprint or planning commitments remain and define workflow states, WIP limits, expedite rules, and completion criteria.

flow.title: Replenish ready work
flow.description: Select work according to product priority and available capacity instead of filling every person or promising a fixed item count.

flow.title: Pull and manage flow
flow.description: Team members pull work, swarm on aging or blocked items, and protect the current goal while handling explicit service classes.

flow.title: Review outcomes and flow
flow.description: Inspect delivered value, goal achievement, cycle time, throughput, and policy effectiveness; then adapt the system.

roles: Existing product and delivery roles remain in place
A flow facilitator or service owner may support policies, replenishment, and reviews
strengths: Can reduce Scrum carryover and multitasking
Handles planned and unplanned work more transparently
Supports gradual process evolution
risks: May inherit the weaknesses of both systems
Ambiguous rules make forecasting and accountability worse
Teams may retain ceremonies that no longer serve a purpose
healthySignals: The team can explain every cadence and policy
Work-in-progress limits change behavior
Goals and service demand are balanced explicitly

title: Lean Product and Delivery
summary: A management approach that improves value by understanding the full value stream, creating flow and pull, reducing waste, and continuously improving the system.
description: Lean asks teams to define value from the customer perspective and optimize the whole path by which that value is created. It is not simply cost cutting. In digital work it influences small batches, quality at the source, fast feedback, value-stream analysis, and respect for the people closest to the work.
bestFor: Organizations with delay and handoff across an end-to-end service
Teams able to study demand, value, quality, and flow together
Products that benefit from smaller batches and rapid learning
avoidWhen: Leadership treats lean only as headcount or cost reduction
Local utilization targets prevent improvement of the whole value stream
coreIdeas: Specify customer value precisely
Map the end-to-end value stream
Create smooth flow and use pull instead of excess inventory
Pursue perfection through continuous learning and respect for people

flow.title: Define value
flow.description: Identify the customer, the outcome they value, and the quality and timing conditions that make the service useful.

flow.title: Map the value stream
flow.description: Visualize every meaningful step, delay, handoff, rework loop, and information dependency from demand to delivered value.

flow.title: Improve flow and pull
flow.description: Reduce batch size, queues, rework, and unnecessary handoffs while starting work according to actual demand and capacity.

flow.title: Learn toward perfection
flow.description: Use repeated experiments, quality feedback, and frontline knowledge to improve the entire system rather than blame individuals.

roles: No mandatory roles are prescribed by Lean thinking
Leadership and frontline contributors jointly improve the value stream and remove waste
strengths: Optimizes the whole service rather than one department
Makes queues, rework, and non-value work visible
Connects quality and learning to everyday operations
risks: Can be reduced to efficiency theater
Waste language may be applied carelessly to people or necessary resilience
Local optimization can damage customer value
healthySignals: Lead time and rework improve with maintained quality
People closest to work shape improvements
Customer value guides trade-offs

references.name: Lean Enterprise Institute: What is Lean Thinking?

title: Extreme Programming
summary: An agile software-development method that combines short feedback cycles with disciplined engineering practices such as test-first development, pairing, refactoring, and continuous integration.
description: Extreme Programming addresses a gap that process conversations often miss: the technical ability to change software safely. Practices reinforce one another, so adopting only a daily meeting or isolated test technique does not create XP. Teams tailor responsibly while preserving rapid feedback and shared code quality.
bestFor: Software products with changing requirements and frequent delivery
Teams able to collaborate closely with users and one another
Codebases where automated feedback and design improvement are valuable
avoidWhen: Management demands rapid scope change but rejects engineering investment
Pairing, testing, and integration are imposed mechanically without team understanding
coreIdeas: Take valuable work in very small steps
Use automated tests and continuous integration for rapid feedback
Improve design continuously through refactoring
Share knowledge through pairing, collective ownership, and close customer communication

flow.title: Select a small valuable story
flow.description: Clarify a user-facing slice and acceptance examples small enough to design, implement, and validate quickly.

flow.title: Test and design collaboratively
flow.description: Use tests, simple design, pairing, and shared discussion to make intended behavior and technical choices explicit before overbuilding.

flow.title: Integrate continuously
flow.description: Commit small changes frequently, keep the build healthy, and resolve integration problems immediately.

flow.title: Get feedback and refactor
flow.description: Review behavior with the customer, improve code structure without changing behavior, and use learning to select the next small story.

strengths: Builds technical capacity for safe change
Spreads code ownership and knowledge
Makes quality feedback immediate
risks: Practices can be copied without their reinforcing system
Pairing can fail without safety and skill
Insufficient product access weakens fast feedback
healthySignals: The main branch remains releasable
Refactoring and tests keep change cost manageable
Knowledge is shared rather than concentrated

title: DevOps Lifecycle
summary: A continuous product and operational lifecycle that joins planning, building, testing, delivery, operation, observation, and improvement through shared ownership and automation.
description: DevOps is a socio-technical approach rather than a handoff from developers to a tool-owning team. Effective implementations improve both delivery performance and operational outcomes through version control, continuous integration, deployment automation, observability, security, learning, and healthy collaboration.
bestFor: Digital products requiring frequent safe change
Teams willing to share delivery and operational feedback
Organizations investing in platforms, automation, and learning
avoidWhen: A separate DevOps team is expected to absorb every operational responsibility
Speed is pursued without quality, security, resilience, or user outcomes
coreIdeas: Share responsibility from product idea through operation
Automate repeatable build, test, infrastructure, and deployment work
Use small batches and continuous feedback
Learn from telemetry and incidents without blame

flow.title: Plan and design
flow.description: Frame outcomes, risks, architecture, operational needs, and a small releasable change with cross-functional input.

flow.title: Build and verify continuously
flow.description: Use version control, automated builds, tests, security checks, and review to keep changes integrated and releasable.

flow.title: Release safely
flow.description: Promote repeatable artifacts through environments using automated controls, progressive strategies, approvals where needed, and rollback readiness.

flow.title: Operate and observe
flow.description: Monitor technical and user outcomes, respond to incidents, and compare real behavior with expectations and service objectives.

flow.title: Improve the system
flow.description: Turn delivery metrics, incidents, user evidence, and developer friction into prioritized product, platform, and process improvements.

strengths: Shortens feedback from change to real operation
Improves repeatability and shared ownership
Connects product delivery with reliability and security
risks: Tool adoption may be mistaken for culture and capability
Automation can accelerate unsafe designs
Unmanaged cognitive load can overwhelm product teams
healthySignals: Changes move in small safe batches
Recovery and learning improve alongside delivery frequency
Teams can observe and own their services

title: Double Diamond Design Process
summary: A design process that separates discovering the right problem from defining it, then exploring possible solutions before converging on delivery.
description: The Double Diamond makes divergent and convergent thinking visible across Discover, Define, Develop, and Deliver. It is not necessarily a rigid linear sequence; teams revisit evidence and decisions. Its value is protecting problem understanding and alternative exploration from premature commitment to a polished solution.
bestFor: Unclear user problems or service opportunities
Cross-functional discovery and design work
Teams needing a shared map from evidence to delivery
avoidWhen: The process is treated as four mandatory handoff departments
Research is performed but cannot influence the brief or solution
coreIdeas: Diverge before converging on a problem definition
Base the brief on evidence from people and context
Explore multiple solution directions before selecting
Test, deliver, and learn rather than treating launch as the end

flow.title: Discover
flow.description: Explore people, context, systems, existing evidence, constraints, and opportunities broadly before deciding what the problem is.

flow.title: Define
flow.description: Synthesize findings into a focused problem, outcome, audience, constraints, and decision brief that the team can act on.

flow.title: Develop
flow.description: Generate and prototype multiple approaches, test assumptions, and combine useful ideas without converging too early.

flow.title: Deliver
flow.description: Refine, implement, validate, launch, and monitor the selected solution while retaining feedback loops for further change.

roles: No prescribed roles are required by the framework
Research, design, product, engineering, users, and stakeholders usually participate
strengths: Protects problem discovery from premature solution fixation
Makes divergent and convergent work understandable
Supports cross-functional design and innovation
risks: Can be misread as a one-way waterfall
Diamonds may become presentation theater without real evidence
Delivery realities may be excluded until too late
healthySignals: The problem definition changes when discovery evidence requires it
Multiple options are explored before commitment
Launch produces evidence for another learning cycle

title: Shape Up Product Development
summary: A product-development method that shapes bounded problems before betting on them, gives teams fixed time and variable scope, and separates building cycles from cooldown.
description: Shape Up organizes work around appetites rather than detailed estimates. Senior shapers define the problem, boundaries, risks, and rough solution; decision-makers choose bets; small autonomous teams build within a fixed cycle and cut scope when necessary. It is designed for particular organizational conditions, not as a universal replacement for product discovery or delivery management.
bestFor: Mature product teams able to work autonomously
Organizations willing to fix time while varying scope
Product work that can be shaped into bounded meaningful bets
avoidWhen: Teams require daily assignment or fixed detailed scope
Critical dependencies and operational demand cannot be isolated within a cycle
coreIdeas: Set an appetite before designing the solution
Shape enough to remove major unknowns without writing a task specification
Bet on a few bounded projects instead of maintaining one giant priority queue
Give builders autonomy and cut scope rather than extending the cycle

flow.title: Shape the work
flow.description: Define the problem, appetite, solution elements, rabbit holes, and explicit no-gos at the right level of abstraction.

flow.title: Betting table
flow.description: Decision-makers compare shaped pitches, capacity, strategy, and risks, then commit teams without carrying an automatic backlog.

flow.title: Build in a fixed cycle
flow.description: A small autonomous team discovers tasks, integrates scopes, manages risk, and delivers the core within the fixed timebox.

flow.title: Cooldown and learn
flow.description: Teams address small fixes, explore ideas, and prepare for future work while the organization reviews what shipped and what was learned.

strengths: Protects teams from constant reprioritization
Encourages bounded problems and autonomous execution
Makes time fixed and scope negotiable
risks: Poorly shaped bets transfer hidden risk to builders
The model can underrepresent continuous support and compliance work
Central betting decisions may distance teams from ongoing user evidence
healthySignals: Pitches expose risks and no-gos before commitment
Teams cut scope while preserving the core outcome
Cycles finish with meaningful integrated work
